items.text: Round 1 resolved all five top-level decisions: (a) d1=C — migrate existing intro_anomaly_log rows into payment_anomaly_log and drop the old table (plan now reflects migrate+drop instead of the freeze strategy it originally drafted); (b) d2=A — generic JSON payload only; (c) d3=A — conservative rate-limit defaults (burst=5, refill=1/60s); (d) d4=A — webhook URL treated as a secret via the reveal endpoint; (e) d5=A — fire-and-forget dispatch, no sweeper. Round 2 focuses on the remaining implementation mechanics that d1=C and d5=A expose: migration logistics, async test synchronization, goroutine lifecycle, and config hot-reload semantics.

items.context: Round 1 d1=C chose to migrate existing intro_anomaly_log rows into payment_anomaly_log and drop the old table. We need to decide WHEN the migration runs. intro_anomaly_log has 6 columns (id, email, customer_id, coupon_id, anomaly_type, details, created_at); payment_anomaly_log has 12. The column mapping (§8g in plan.md) fills defaults: severity='warn', subject_id=coupon_id, subject_kind='intro_coupon', dispatch_status='skipped' (historical rows are not re-dispatched). The remaining choice is execution model: in-band with app migrations, or a separate manual step.

options.label: Boot-time transactional migration: on API start, after CREATE TABLE runs, execute the `DO $$ ... END $$` block from §8g as a statement in the existing `stmts []string` migration slice. Idempotent via the `information_schema` guard, so re-runs on already-migrated DBs no-op.
options.rationale: Zero operator friction — upgrade happens automatically on deploy. Single transaction (DO $$ BEGIN ... END $$) guarantees atomicity. Matches the existing pattern where all schema migrations live inline in main.go's stmts slice. Idempotent on re-run. Covered by integration tests.

options.label: Standalone SQL script + boot guard: ship `docs/internal/migrations/001-intro-anomaly-log-merge.sql` and have ops run it once. API code checks at startup that intro_anomaly_log does not exist; if it does, log a loud error and refuse to start.
options.rationale: Explicit operator control; easier to inspect and review the migration before running. Adds a manual step to the release checklist and a boot-time hard-fail if the ops step is missed — riskier for small-team deploys.

options.label: Background migration worker: on first boot after the new table exists, spawn a goroutine that copies rows in batches (1000 at a time) and drops the source table at the end. Boot is not blocked.
options.rationale: Useful if intro_anomaly_log has millions of rows and would slow boot significantly. Overkill for LPBS today (intro_anomaly_log currently has ≤ a few hundred rows in any deployment). Adds concurrency concerns (what if the dispatcher is already inserting into payment_anomaly_log while the copy runs?).

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Specify a different migration approach (e.g., separate tool, multi-step with verification before DROP).

items.topic: Test-time synchronization for the async dispatcher
items.context: `PaymentAnomalyService.Log()` fires dispatch on a goroutine (round-1 d5=A fire-and-forget). Integration tests need a deterministic way to assert that dispatch happened, what the POST body was, and whether retries ran — all without `time.Sleep()` or racing. This design choice shapes every dispatcher test and affects what test-only code (if any) lives in production source files.

options.label: `WaitForDispatch(ctx, rowID)` helper on the service: polls the row's `dispatch_status` column (`pending` → `sent`/`skipped`/`failed`) until it transitions or ctx times out. Tests call `id, _ := svc.Log(...)` then `svc.WaitForDispatch(ctx, id)` to block until the async path finishes. Used only in tests but lives in production code so it has a real code path.
options.rationale: Explicit, race-free. Uses the dispatch_status column that already exists for normal operation — no test-only branches. Operators can also call it from admin tools to confirm a manual insert dispatched. Clean separation of concerns.

options.label: Sync-mode flag: `PaymentAnomalyServiceOptions{SyncDispatch: true}` on construction. Tests set the flag; `Log()` dispatches synchronously before returning. Production always constructs with SyncDispatch=false.
options.rationale: Simplest test code (`Log()` returns after dispatch). Introduces a production/test code divergence — the sync path is never exercised in prod, so async-only bugs (e.g., ctx cancellation races) can slip through. Small but real risk.

options.label: Dispatcher `Done()` channel: dispatcher exposes a channel that receives the row id after each dispatch completes. Tests drain the channel with `select` + timeout.
options.rationale: Race-free but threading a channel through the API for a test-only concern is awkward. Breaks down with concurrent test dispatches (how does a test know which message is for its anomaly?).

items.context: Each `Log()` call spawns a dispatch goroutine. Without any bound, a flood of anomalies (e.g., a detection bug) could spawn hundreds of goroutines simultaneously against a slow webhook endpoint. The rate limiter already caps spawn rate per-type, but a poorly-distributed burst across many types could still pile up. Plan §11 lists 'goroutine leak on shutdown' as low-risk; this decision nails down the concrete lifecycle model.

options.label: Unbounded goroutines tied to shutdown context: every dispatch spawns via `go func() { ... }()` with the server's shutdown context. Relies on rate limiter (burst=5, refill=1/60s per type) + 5s HTTP timeout + max 3 retries to bound in-flight work.
options.rationale: Simplest. Math: rate limiter caps ~5 goroutines per type per minute; across ~10 anomaly types, worst-case steady-state is ~50 concurrent goroutines, each exiting within ~7s (3 attempts * 5s + 2s backoff). No pool lifecycle to manage. Matches how StripeService handles reconciliation fan-out today.

options.label: Bounded worker pool: a fixed-size pool of N=8 workers drains from a buffered channel (size 64). `Log()` enqueues; workers dispatch. If the channel is full, `Log()` marks the row `dispatch_status='overflow'` and does not block.
options.rationale: Hard upper bound on concurrent dispatches (8). Adds pool lifecycle management, a new `dispatch_status` value (`overflow`), and channel overflow handling. Overkill given the rate limiter already constrains spawn rate and 'overflow' would only hit in detection-bug scenarios that are not yet real.

options.label: Single-worker queue: one long-running goroutine drains all dispatches serially from an unbounded channel. `Log()` writes to the channel non-blocking via `select { case ch <- row: default: mark 'overflow' }`.
options.rationale: Maximally simple concurrency bound (=1). Serializes dispatches — a slow webhook (3 attempts × 5s = 15s) stalls the entire queue, so alerts for different types can't go in parallel. Bad tail latency for guardrail alerts.

items.topic: Config hot-reload semantics for the dispatcher
items.context: When an admin PATCHes the Stripe settings, the dispatcher's in-memory config (webhook URL, enabled flag, per-type rate limits) must be updated without a redeploy. Plan §7 Phase 4 step 4 mentions `paymentAnomalyService.RefreshConfig(ctx)` but does not pin down whether it's called on PATCH, lazily on each dispatch, or on a TTL. This affects admin UX (how fast do settings take effect?) and code complexity.

options.label: Push on PATCH: `handleUpdateStripeSettings` calls `paymentAnomalyService.RefreshConfig(ctx)` after a successful save. Dispatcher holds config in an `atomic.Pointer[anomalyConfig]`; readers load the pointer with one atomic op.
options.rationale: Predictable: after a save, next dispatch uses new config. Near-zero overhead (refresh runs only on PATCH, not per dispatch). Matches how StripeService already handles RefreshConfig after its settings PATCH — consistent pattern operators already understand. Integration test (`TestUpdate_RefreshesAnomalyConfig`) is a direct assertion.

options.label: Pull per dispatch: dispatcher reads settings fresh from the DB on every `Dispatch()` call.
options.rationale: Always fresh, no stale window. Adds a DB round-trip per dispatch (cheap, but wasteful and violates 'batching DB reads' convention). Does not match the StripeService pattern — divergence is surprising.

options.label: Pull on TTL: dispatcher caches config for 30s, refreshes from DB when stale.
options.rationale: Upper bound on staleness; one fewer seam to wire through. 30s admin-observability lag is acceptable but worse UX than push (operator saves, then has to wait up to 30s to see the new webhook URL fire). Adds a time-based cache — another moving part to test.

plan_updates: Round 1 decisions (d1-d5) all resolved. Updated plan.md to incorporate d1=C (migrate + drop intro_anomaly_log): Phase 1 now includes a one-time INSERT-then-DROP DO $$ block migration (idempotent, information_schema-guarded); Phase 3 simplified (no coexistence logic, no dual-write); §8g added with explicit migration SQL and column mapping; Target End State item 4, Rollout Checklist, Risks matrix (removed freeze-era concern, added migration-failure risk), Non-goals (added 'no dual-write, no union view'), and Definition of Done (items 3 and 7) all updated. Also added `atomic.Pointer[anomalyConfig]` and `sync.Mutex` bucket guarding to the service sketch in §7 Phase 2 / §8d for concreteness. Round 2 asks four implementation-mechanics decisions (migration timing, async test sync, goroutine lifecycle, config refresh) that will move approach_solid/testable/risk_awareness from 2 to 3 once resolved.
